title: The Whoopi Monologues at Lincoln Center #thewhoopimonologues #karayou...
transcript: Long before icon and EGOT winner Whoopi Goldberg became a mainstay of The View, her stage career was first defined by a series of one-woman shows, such as this one currently being revived at Lincoln Center. It's a set of five distinct monologues, each from a different character navigating some personal hardship or reckoning — an unexpected pregnancy, a new job in a new place, or a yearning to look like a movie star, for example. Both funny and sad, the piece highlights the humanity of people and experiences often overlooked and underacknowledged. Unlike the original 1984 production, this one distributes the material among five actresses. I wasn't alive to see it the first time around, so I can't speak to what is lost by removing the element of solo performance, though I have my suspicions. Regardless, the assured and glossy direction by Whitney White never makes you question why there are five performers here instead of one. The way the actresses who aren't currently monologuing are occasionally incorporated isn't always graceful, but to me it represents the universality of our experiences. While some monologues are more impactful than others, all five actresses have the comedic sensibilities to hold the room effortlessly and integrate some light crowd work into their performances, again highlighting the communal aspect of the material. Perhaps my only critique is that two-time Tony Award winner Kara Young sets too high of a bar as the show's opener — she's simply too good. With that, another Playbill for my collection.
classificationReason: Creator offers detailed first-hand critical analysis of the production — direction by Whitney White, the choice to use five actresses instead of one, individual performances, and the impact of specific monologues — indicating they attended and are sharing a personal opinion.
